articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License for Iraq Development Bank
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License FF-1. This license authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank, and certain entities majority-owned by it.

The amended General License FF-1, effective October 29, 2026, replaces and supersedes the previous General License FF. A key provision of the new license requires that any payments to blocked persons must be made into blocked accounts.
This action by OFAC aims to provide a structured process for the cessation of certain financial activities while ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions against Iran.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entity for North Korea IT Worker Schemes and Sanctions Rwanda for DRC Support
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for their involvement in Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes. These schemes defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the DPRK's unlawful weapons programs.

In a separate action, OFAC also announced Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations. The Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution, were sanctioned for facilitating Rwanda's support for the M23 movement in eastern DRC.

These designations underscore Treasury's commitment to disrupting illicit financial networks supporting North Korea's WMD programs and holding accountable those who destabilize the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to resolve potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of Russia sanctions. The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer.
OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. The settlement amount for Extreme Networks, Inc. is $1,529,685.
This enforcement action highlights the importance of robust compliance programs, especially for companies operating in sectors with heightened sanctions risks related to Russia.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update aims to provide clearer guidance to financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations.
The amended FAQs address various scenarios and offer clarifications on the procedures for handling blocked property and rejected transactions, as well as the reporting requirements to OFAC.
This issuance is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to enhance transparency and assist the public in understanding and adhering to U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. Concurrently, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

In addition to these designation changes, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses. These licenses provide authorizations for specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs.

The agency also published amended Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance on these new actions and existing sanctions programs, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target entities and individuals involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property rights.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC has issued associated General Licenses. These licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences of the sanctions by authorizing certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited.
This action reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American intellectual property and holding accountable those who engage in its theft or misappropriation.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela.

Alongside the amended General License, OFAC also published an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This FAQ provides additional clarification and guidance on the scope and application of the amended license.

These adjustments reflect the ongoing recalibration of U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela, aiming to address specific humanitarian or economic considerations while maintaining pressure on the Maduro regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. Concurrently, OFAC also imposed a new designation related to Cuba.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses. These licenses aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited by the new sanctions.
The agency also published updated Frequently Asked Questions to offer further guidance and clarity on the scope and implications of these recent actions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action signifies a change in the sanctions status of a previously designated individual or entity.
Designation removals typically occur when the underlying reasons for the designation no longer apply, or when there has been a change in circumstances that warrants such an action.
This removal reflects a specific adjustment within the broader framework of U.S. sanctions against Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of those engaged in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating global illicit activities that pose threats to national security and international stability.
These measures are part of a broader strategy to isolate and incapacitate criminal and terrorist organizations by cutting off their access to the international financial system.

articles.headline: UNESCO Reports Rising Impunity for Journalist Killings, Drones Emerge as New Threat
body: Global impunity for journalist killings has risen for the first time in over a decade, reaching 86% in 2024-2025, according to the latest report from UNESCO. This increase coincides with a 20% rise in journalist fatalities, with 189 journalists and media workers killed during the period, the highest number since 2014-2015.

A disturbing new trend identified in the report is the growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), or drones, to kill journalists, particularly in conflict zones. Fifty journalists, representing 40% of those killed in conflict areas, died due to drone strikes.

Despite the grim global picture, impunity in non-conflict countries has steadily declined, falling from 94% in 2012 to 77% in 2026, demonstrating that targeted investigations and protections can yield positive results.

articles.headline: US Diverges from Global Approach on Emergency Preparedness, Focuses on Military Response
body: While governments worldwide are launching campaigns to encourage public preparedness for emergencies like cyber-attacks and natural disasters, the United States is adopting a different strategy, focusing primarily on military preparation rather than civilian readiness.

Countries such as the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Japan have issued updated guidance urging their populations to stock up on supplies for at least 72 hours in case of crisis or war. These initiatives reflect growing concerns about climate change, technological dependency, and hostile state threats.

Emergency experts in the U.S. acknowledge the increasing threat of cyber-attacks and the compounding risks of natural and human-made disasters, highlighting a potential gap in the nation's overall emergency preparedness strategy.

articles.headline: Israeli Arab Coalition Leader Sees 'Historic Opportunity' for Change After Elections
body: The leader of Israel's main Palestinian coalition, Yousef Jabareen, has stated that the country faces a 'historic opportunity' to change direction following recent elections. His Joint List now holds the balance of power in the Knesset.

Jabareen expressed readiness to join forces with the 'Change' bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition. Turnout among Arab Israelis, who constitute 20% of the population, more than doubled to approximately 80%, significantly altering the political landscape.

A primary demand of Palestinian Israeli voters is the removal of the Netanyahu government, particularly its most extreme members. Jabareen also voiced concern that Netanyahu might initiate war with Iran as a pretext to delay political transition.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Moves to Commerce Control List
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced that, effective November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms. Under the new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons.

License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors. Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security Jeffrey I. Kessler stated that this move alleviates compliance burdens on the firearms industry while maintaining national security.

articles.headline: DHS Adds Chinese Genomics Companies to UFLPA Entity List Over Forced Labor Concerns
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), as Chair of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), has announced additions to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List, effective October 29, 2026. Three Chinese genomics companies, BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., MGI Tech Co., Ltd., and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (BGI Group), have been added to the list.

These entities are identified under sections of the UFLPA that target companies working with the Xinjiang government to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor, or those that source material from Xinjiang for forced labor programs.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will now apply a rebuttable presumption that goods produced by these entities are prohibited from entering the United States. This action aims to eliminate threats to American businesses from foreign competitors' unfair practices and uphold human dignity.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah (bank), for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.
